options: How the WORK GROWS as the input grows - machine and constants ignored
explanation: The shape of the curve, not the speed of the box. An O(n) algorithm on a slow machine still beats O(n squared) once n is large enough.
The inner loop runs fully per outer pass: n x n. (Sequential loops ADD, staying O(n).)
Rule 5: halving means log. 1,000,000 halves to 1 in ~20 steps - the shape behind binary search.

options: O(n squared) - drop constants AND lower terms
explanation: Constants do not change the curve's shape; n squared dominates n as n grows. Only the fastest-growing term survives.

stem: The lesson quadruples the data and linear search gets ~4x slower while binary search barely moves. Because:
options: O(n) scales with n; O(log n) needs only TWO extra comparisons for 4x data
explanation: log2(4n) = log2(n) + 2. The curve shapes made physical - a billion sorted items need just 30 comparisons.

options: WORST - the guarantee you can plan around
explanation: Linear search's best case is 1 step, but you design for the n-step worst. When average and worst differ wildly (quicksort), state both.

options: O(1) means CONSTANT - one slow fixed step is still O(1)
explanation: Constant = independent of n, not quick. Conversely a big constant inside O(n) can beat O(log n) at small n - measure (6.2).

stem: for (i..n) if (list.Contains(x)) - the real complexity is:
options: O(n squared) - Contains is itself an O(n) loop
explanation: The classic ACCIDENTAL quadratic (3.2): the inner loop hides in a method call. A HashSet makes each check O(1).

stem: Merge sort is O(n log n) time but needs O(n) SPACE because:
options: Merging requires temporary arrays; bubble sort sorts in place at O(1) extra
explanation: Time and space both get the notation - and often trade against each other (5.4's memoisation buys time with memory).

stem: An O(2 to the n) algorithm at n=50, if n=20 took one second, takes roughly:
options: A BILLION seconds - each +1 doubles the work
explanation: 2 to the 30 more work is about 10 to the 9. This is naive Fibonacci's fate (5.4), and why exponential algorithms are 'hopeless' beyond toy sizes.
